comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira and considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management. The key reason someone would switch is to take advantage of Plane's self-hosted and free features.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Plane is free and self-hosted, while Jira has a per-user monthly cost.
* Data ownership: Plane allows full data ownership since it's self-hosted, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical setup, while Jira offers a simpler, cloud-based setup.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large-scale enterprises, while Plane is more suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Jira has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited but growing list of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
  + Extensive integration library
  + Scalable for large enterprises
  + User-friendly interface
  + Robust customer support
  + Wide range of features
* Cons:
  + Expensive for small teams
  + Limited customization options
  + Data storage concerns
  + Steep learning curve
**Plane:**
* Pros:
  + Free and self-hosted
  + Full data ownership
  + Customizable
  + Growing community
  + Simple and intuitive interface
* Cons:
  + Limited integrations
  + Technical setup required
  + Limited scalability
  + Limited customer support
  + Still in development

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large enterprises with complex project management needs, requiring a wide range of integrations and a scalable solution. It's also suitable for teams that prioritize a user-friendly interface and robust customer support. On the other hand, Plane is ideal for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership, customization, and a free, self-hosted solution. Teams with technical expertise and a willingness to contribute to the Plane community may also find it an attractive option.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use the Plane import tool to migrate your data.
3. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira setup.
4. Test and verify that all data has been successfully migrated.
5. Update any integrations or workflows to work with Plane.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it's still in the development phase and lacks some key features. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane currently lacks support for certain types of custom fields, which may be a deal-breaker for some teams. However, for small to medium-sized teams with simple project management needs, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira, offering a free and self-hosted solution with full data ownership.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need extensive integrations
* Individuals or solo developers who value data ownership and customization
* Teams with technical expertise who can handle Plane's setup and maintenance
* Organizations with limited budgets who can't afford Jira's per-user costs
* Teams who prioritize simplicity and a lightweight project management solution

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, with no per-user costs.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Does Plane have the same features as Jira?
No, Plane currently lacks some features and integrations compared to Jira.
### Is Plane suitable for large enterprises?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large enterprises due to its limited scalability and lack of certain features.
### Can I customize Plane to fit my team's needs?
Yes, Plane is highly customizable, allowing teams to tailor it to their specific needs.

title: Trello vs WeKan

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are two popular project management tools used for organizing and tracking tasks. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary, cloud-based solution to a self-hosted, open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is to manage projects using boards, lists, and cards, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: WeKan requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosting, whereas Trello is easy to sign up for and start using.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to scale with large teams and enterprises, while WeKan's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities.
* Integration: Trello has a wider range of integrations with third-party apps and services, including Google Drive and Slack, whereas WeKan has limited integrations but allows for custom development.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $250/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,000/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Trello:**
* Easy to use and intuitive interface
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Scalable and reliable
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data and security
**WeKan:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Customizable and flexible
* Cost-effective for large teams
* Community-driven development
* Limited integrations and support

## When to Choose Each
Trello is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use project management tool with a wide range of integrations. It's ideal for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay for the convenience of a cloud-based solution. WeKan, on the other hand, is perfect for larger teams or organizations that require self-hosting, customization, and control over their data. It's also suitable for teams with technical expertise and the resources to set up and maintain their own servers.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Trello boards and cards in JSON format using the Trello API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up your WeKan server and configure the necessary settings.
3. Use the WeKan import tool to import your Trello data in JSON format.
4. Customize your WeKan setup to fit your team's needs.
5. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly.

## Our Take
WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and configure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for teams that require self-hosting and control over their data, WeKan is a great alternative to Trello, and we recommend switching to WeKan if you have the technical resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with technical expertise that don't need integrations with third-party apps
* Medium-sized teams that require self-hosting and control over their data
* Large teams with the resources to set up and maintain their own servers
* Teams that don't need mobile apps or a wide range of integrations
* Organizations that require customization and flexibility in their project management tool

## FAQ
### Can I self-host WeKan on my own server?
Yes, WeKan is designed to be self-hosted, and you can install it on your own server.
### Is WeKan free?
Yes, WeKan is completely free and open-source.
### Can I import my Trello data into WeKan?
Yes, you can export your Trello data in JSON format and import it into WeKan using the WeKan import tool.
### Does WeKan have mobile apps?
No, WeKan does not have mobile apps, but it has a responsive web interface that can be accessed on mobile devices.
### Is WeKan scalable?
WeKan's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Dropbox is one of the original cloud storage services offering simple file sync. Nextcloud is the most popular self-hosted cloud platform combining file storage, calendar, contacts, video calls, and 400+ apps.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Dropbox charges $9.99-$16.58/user/month; Nextcloud is free to self-host
- **Storage**: Nextcloud storage is limited only by your server disk space
- **Feature breadth**: Nextcloud is far more than storage; it is a full Google Workspace alternative
- **Privacy**: Nextcloud on your own server means only you can access your data
- **Setup**: Dropbox is instant; Nextcloud requires Docker setup

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$500/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,998/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Dropbox

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Dropbox if:** Dropbox suits individuals or small teams wanting simple reliable file sync with no infrastructure to manage.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud suits privacy-focused organizations wanting to eliminate cloud subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Download all Dropbox files locally, then upload to Nextcloud via the web interface or desktop sync client.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Dropbox tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Dropbox, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Dropbox until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Dropbox paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Dropbox data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Dropbox](https://dropbox.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Nextcloud is a free, self-hosted alternative to Dropbox. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two database management tools that help teams organize and manage their data. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and scalable database solution, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user per month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows for full data ownership since it is self-hosted, while Airtable stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more straightforward setup process, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both tools are scalable, but NocoDB's self-hosted nature allows for more flexibility in scaling.
* Integration difference: Airtable has native integration with a wider range of third-party apps, while NocoDB has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Airtable
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
	+ Scalable and reliable
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Limited control over data ownership
	+ Can be expensive for large teams
	+ Limited flexibility in customization
### NocoDB
* Pros:
	+ Self-hosted and free
	+ Full control over data ownership
	+ Highly customizable
	+ Scalable and flexible
* Cons:
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Limited integrations with third-party apps
	+ Still a relatively new tool with some bugs and limitations
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for teams that need a straightforward and easy-to-use database solution with a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that do not require full control over their data ownership. On the other hand, NocoDB is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data ownership and are looking for a self-hosted solution.
